newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK property seen buoyant under China.
newsitem.headline: HK property seen buoyant under China.

text.p: Hong Kong's last colonial land auction has signalled that the property market will remain strong under Chinese rule but a more restrained pace of growth is expected under the new government, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Hong Kong does not want prices to come down very sharply, nor does it want prices to go up by too much," said Michael Green, property analyst at Salomon Brothers.
"I think it is going to adopt a very practical policy based on providing enough supply for the people and also a policy that will please the developers as well," he said.

After 156 years of colonial rule, Britain will hand Hong Kong back to China at midnight on June 30. The present government held its final land auction before the change in sovereignty on Tuesday, drawing a mixed response from property developers but ultimately one which showed continued confidence in Hong Kong's real estate market.

A remote plot of land in Stanley, on the southern side of Hong Kong island, sold for a lower-than-expected HK$5.5 billion (US$711 million) but the sale of a residential site in Kowloon's Hunghom drew more enthusiasm and sold above expectations at HK$6.06 billion.
"It is now very clear that the prospects for higher residential prices for 1997 is a distinct likelihood," said Michael Leary, senior property analyst at Lehman Brothers.
He raised his growth forecasts by five percent for each of the next two years as a result of the auction, bringing his forecasts to annual growth of 10 to 15 percent.
Analysts said the shortage of supply in Hong Kong's property market guaranteed that prices would continue rising.

But Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa has indicated concern over spiralling real estate prices, which surged about 30 percent in 1996 and are forecast to rise by another 20 to 30 percent this year.

Analysts said the appointment of real estate tycoon C.Y. Leung at the head of a post-colonial committee to map out long-term housing strategy would mean policy would be focused on the supply side rather than policies to rein in demand.
"We are going to see an increase in the supply of land," said Martin Tacon, senior associate at CS First Boston.

Although more land supply would not have an immediate impact, due to the time lag between converting the land for development use, releasing it and building on it, he said property prices would eventually rise at a lower pace.
Peter Churchouse, regional strategist at Morgan Stanley, said housing supply should grow to around 35,000-36,000 units next year from about 26,000-27,000 units this year.

"We can easily absorb 35,000 to 36,000 and still be an environment where prices will probably edge up," he said. "If they can get supply up to 35,000 that will take the sting out of this market and mean speculators will be less active."

Churchouse said price increases of inflation plus five to 10 percent would be sustainable. "That will improve affordability but developers will have the opportunity to make considerable gains," he said.
Property developers could maintain earnings growth simply by selling more units amid strong demand and targeting the higher end of the market, analysts said.
Leary predicted earnings growth of just under 20 percent for the industry over the next two years. "That is well above the Hang Seng Index and stronger than other sectors in the market."
Property stocks have underperformed the Hang Seng Index by about 11 percent this year and that should stop once future property policy becomes clearer, Leary said.
"You are getting good earnings delivery which is why the underperformance is somewhat surprising. That should reverse when the current situation is resolved." (US$1 = HK$7.74)
